system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were admitted to the hospital on February 3, 2020, and discharged on May 9, 2020. You stayed for 3 months, 6 days, and 7 hours.

You were referred to the hospital because you had a cough for 4 weeks that was dry, meaning no phlegm came out, and you had night sweats. You also mentioned that 3 days before coming to the hospital, you had a fever (you didn't measure it) and dyspnea (difficulty breathing). One day before coming, you suddenly felt pain on the right side of your chest, which spread to your right neck area, and your breathing difficulty got much worse. You said you didn't cough up any blood. You also mentioned that you were in prison for about 3 years, and for 6 years you had no symptoms. You also reported losing about 8 kg of weight about a month ago, but you didn't know the exact amount. You didn't have any problems with your urine or motions (bowel movements).

When you were examined, your general condition was regular. You looked a bit pale, but you were hydrated (had enough fluids), not bluish (acyanotic), not yellow (anicteric), and you were conscious and knew where you were. Your heart sounds were normal, with a heart rate of 85 beats per minute. When your lungs were checked, breathing sounds were heard on the left side of your chest, but not on the right side, and your chest didn't expand equally on both sides. Your oxygen saturation (amount of oxygen in your blood) was 98%. Your abdomen (belly) was flat, bowel sounds were present, it was soft, and there were no signs of peritonism (inflammation in the belly). Your hands and feet had no swelling (edema), no signs of deep vein thrombosis (blood clots in deep veins), and blood flow to your limbs was good. Your surgical wound was in good condition and dry, with stitches that had not opened up.

You were diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis (TB, an infection in the lungs) in 2019, and the treatment started on February 7, 2020, and ended on April 7, 2020. Tests showed that the TB bacteria were sensitive to the usual medicines.

You had several complications in your lungs because of the TB:
On February 3, 2020, you had a spontaneous pneumothorax (air leaking into the space around your lung, causing it to collapse) on your right side, and a chest drain (a tube to remove air or fluid from the chest) was put in.
On March 3, 2020, you had a pleurostomy (a surgical opening made in the chest wall to drain fluid or air).
Later, this pleurostomy was closed, but your lung collapsed again.
On March 10, a pleural drainage (a procedure to remove fluid from around the lung) was done, and a Heimlich valve (a one-way valve attached to a chest drain to let air out but not in) was put in.
On March 27, the Heimlich valve was removed, but the drain was kept open for the ostomy (the opening).
On March 31, a new pleurotomy (a surgical incision into the pleura, the membrane surrounding the lungs) was performed.
On April 7, an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (a surgery to open the chest to look inside) was done because of bleeding from tuberculous caverns (holes in the lung caused by TB). There was significant oozing (slow bleeding).
On April 7, the cavity (the hole in the lung) was packed with compresses (pads to stop bleeding).
On April 11, 2020, you had a right pneumonectomy (surgical removal of your entire right lung) through a lateral thoracotomy (an incision on the side of the chest). You also had a tracheostomy (a surgical opening in the windpipe to help with breathing). These procedures went smoothly.
Both the chest drain and the tracheostomy were removed on June 6.

You also developed surgical wound infections (infections in the cuts made during surgery) caused by a type of bacteria called Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (a bacteria that is hard to treat with many antibiotics). This was treated with antibiotics: vancomycin, meropenem, and amikacin. This antibiotic treatment was stopped on April 2, after you showed clinical improvement (got better) and your procalcitonin (a blood test marker for infection) level was 0.09.

On April 7, you had hypovolemic shock (a dangerous condition caused by severe blood loss) due to bleeding from the surgical wound and pleurostomy, which needed urgent surgery.

On April 10, you had a cardiopulmonary arrest (your heart and breathing stopped) for 4 minutes, which was due to hypoxia (lack of oxygen). This was in asystole (a flat line on the heart monitor, meaning no electrical activity).

For your follow-up appointment, you will continue treatment with RI (likely a TB medication regimen). You have been given prescriptions for 2 months. You will also continue taking oral iron replacement (medicine to increase iron in your body). We had a meeting with [person] and the thoracic surgery team (doctors who operate on the chest) to explain your condition and treatment and answer any questions. [person] understood the instructions and appreciated the care from the team. We have requested some tests for your follow-up appointment. We have scheduled follow-up appointments at [organization] and with the thoracic surgery team. We have told [person] about warning signs to look out for and instructed them to call if they have any concerns. We have provided a report and contacted [organization] for assisted treatment. Your care was managed by the infectious diseases team (doctors who treat infections) and the thoracic surgery team. You are in good general condition and have no complaints.
